claims.text: The baseline high-entropy alloy is currently employed as an intermediate material in plasma-facing reactor components.
The baseline alloy has moderate thermal conductivity.
The baseline alloy has excellent mechanical strength and fracture toughness.
Adding approximately 3 at.% Cu and applying sub-solidus annealing will produce a continuous Cu-enriched phase along grain boundaries.
The resulting structural mediator will be an interconnected Cu-rich grain-boundary network within the primary HEA matrix.
A well-distributed, continuous Cu-rich phase will increase the electron mean free path.
Increasing the electron mean free path will improve the alloy's heat-transfer capability.
The primary HEA matrix will retain its high mechanical strength after Cu addition and annealing.
The Cu-doped and annealed alloy will have 15–20% higher thermal conductivity than the baseline HEA.
The Cu-doped and annealed alloy will retain yield strength within approximately 5% of the undoped alloy's value.
The Cu-doped and annealed alloy will retain fracture toughness within approximately 5% of the undoped alloy's value.
The predicted benefit will hold during cyclic thermal loading from approximately 300 °C to 800 °C.
A temperature range of 300–800 °C is typical of plasma-facing intermediate-layer operating conditions.
The thermal-conductivity benefit depends on formation of a continuous, finely distributed Cu-rich network.
Excessive Cu segregation or isolated Cu precipitates may prevent the intended heat-transfer enhancement.
Excessive Cu segregation or isolated Cu precipitates may compromise mechanical properties.
The hypothesis is falsified if conductivity improves by less than 10% or if yield strength or fracture toughness degrades by more than 5% relative to the baseline.
